details:
We developed is a tool designed to evaluate potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole by analyzing two critical environmental conditions: solar illumination and visibility of Earth.

The project combines lunar topographic data from NASA’s LOLA Digital Elevation Model (DEM) with astronomical calculations using SPICE kernels from NASA/JPL. Our pipeline processes six candidate locations—Mons Malapert, Nobile, Cabeus B, Shackleton, de Gerlache, and Haworth—over a five-year period (2027–2031). It calculates terrain horizons, the Sun’s position, and Earth’s visibility, generating hourly measurements and scientific metrics. The results are then displayed in an interactive web application where users can explore and compare the locations.

The main benefit is that it provides a way to assess environmental conditions that could affect power generation and communication during future lunar missions. Its intended impact is to support preliminary landing-site evaluation and help make more informed decisions about lunar exploration.

We developed the project using Python for data processing and scientific calculations, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the interactive web application, and SPICE for astronomical computations. We also used NASA/JPL datasets and Git/GitHub for version control and collaboration.

Our project's creative aspect is the integration of lunar terrain analysis and astronomical visibility calculations into a single interactive tool. Instead of evaluating illumination or Earth visibility separately, we combine both factors to provide a more complete perspective of each landing site's conditions.

During development, our team considered terrain elevation, local horizons, solar illumination, Earth visibility, time-dependent changes, data accuracy, and the practical needs of future lunar missions.
